messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  (none)

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sixteen months before seeking treatment, Daniel Mercer, a 57-year-old interior designer, was driving home from a client site visit on a rainy late afternoon when another car came through an intersection and struck the driver’s side of his vehicle. He still described the moment with a particular, frozen clarity: the sudden shape of the other car filling his peripheral vision, the blast of metal against metal, the violent lurch of his own body, and the shrieking sound of tires and impact folding into one noise. He had been certain, in the instant before the collision, that he was about to die. Although he survived, the scene remained lodged in him in fragments that felt more immediate than past, especially the sight of cars smashed at odd angles and the sound of traffic braking too hard.

Before the accident, Daniel had thought of himself as steady, capable, and physically dependable. He spent most days moving between showrooms, clients’ homes, and renovation sites, carrying fabric books, climbing stairs, and making quick judgments in busy spaces. Afterward, what unsettled him most was not only that he had almost been killed, but that his own body no longer felt trustworthy to him. He had come to believe that his body had failed him at the crucial moment and could fail him again without warning. In sessions, he said this less as a dramatic statement than as a grim conclusion: he could no longer trust his own body. That idea widened over time into something more global. He spoke about feeling permanently changed for the worse, as if the accident had split his life into a “before” and “after” and left him stranded in the latter. He also described a quieter, painful disorientation when he looked at himself now: a sense that he no longer knew who he was, that the competent, easy-moving man he had once been did not fully feel like him anymore.

His work made it hard to avoid reminders entirely. Driving had always been part of the job, and even when he tried to structure his week to stay close to his office, he still had to pass congested streets, valet lines, and construction zones. A car with a crumpled bumper parked outside a building could stop him in his tracks. He found himself staring too long at damaged vehicles, his stomach dropping as the image fused with the instant before impact. Ordinary car sounds also cut through him with surprising force. A horn, brakes catching sharply outside a client’s townhouse, or the sudden rev of an engine below his office window could make his body jolt before he had time to think. He was particularly unsettled when accidents came up in conversation. If a contractor mentioned a highway pileup or a client casually referred to a recent crash, Daniel felt his attention narrow and his chest tighten, as though the room had become organized around that one subject and he could not safely stay in it.

Over the following months, these reminders became woven into daily life in ways that left him increasingly constricted. He began choosing routes based less on convenience than on where he thought he was least likely to encounter heavy traffic or the aftermath of a collision. He would arrive early to appointments so he could sit inside the building rather than remain in his car listening to passing traffic. At design meetings, if conversation drifted toward news of local accidents, he would excuse himself to take a call or redirect the discussion back to flooring, lighting, anything else. These were small maneuvers, but they accumulated. Colleagues noticed he was less available for site visits across town. One longtime client commented that he seemed distracted and not quite like himself, a remark that stayed with him because it matched what he already feared.

By the time he came to treatment, Daniel’s world had narrowed around these moments of alarm and the meaning he drew from them. Seeing wrecked cars, hearing traffic sounds, or listening to talk of accidents did not feel to him like simple reminders; they seemed to confirm that something in him had been altered in a lasting way. He spoke with particular sadness about the loss of confidence that had once anchored him professionally and personally. Divorced and living alone, he had few places to test whether his view of himself might be incomplete, and instead he increasingly measured himself against the man he had been before the crash and found only damage. What finally brought him in was a recent incident outside a client’s condominium, when the sound of a minor fender-bender on the street made him freeze on the sidewalk, unable for several moments to move toward the entrance. He found that experience humiliating and frightening. More than anything, he said, he was afraid that this was now his permanent self; what he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was some way to feel recognizable to himself again.
